name: Daria Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, political parties, unions or AI firms. This conversation is confidential. Daria, what is a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We take the printed permit, load the van and drive to whatever line has failed. I like finding the actual break and leaving a clear note for the next crew. I get tired of a tidy form that sends us to the wrong pole, so I keep a little notebook in my jacket.

say: I would say **line isolation** and repairs still need trained hands.
I would keep a **printed permit** and check pole numbers before departure.
think: I have **never used AI** and do not expect minor filing changes to cut shifts.
Our **two-month reserve** can cover a missed standby weekend.
do: Keep the normal **repair rota** and check printed permits.
Mark **pole numbers** in my notebook during the first year.
feel: I feel **calm about work** while still watching school costs.
S0.quote: I am not going to guess at an isolation point to save a minute.
fieldNote: Daria prefers a **paper notebook** after seeing two nearly identical pole numbers behind a bakery.
Her **two-month savings** and regular wage make small office changes feel manageable despite mortgage and child costs.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs and verify printed permits and pole numbers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a faster form does not change a fallen line. We still need to isolate the circuit, reach the pole and fit the new section.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never tried AI, and I do not expect a little paperwork saving to change my shifts. We have about two months of expenses saved and the mortgage is paid from my regular wage, so I can leave the emergency fund alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same repair rota and check the printed permit before the van moves. In the first year I would continue marking the pole numbers in my notebook rather than rely on an auto-filled sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about work. My partner and I still budget for the children's school clothes, but a missed standby weekend would not make us miss the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is in the notebook that the form misses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the lane behind the bakery, two poles have almost the same number because one was replaced. My note says which old base is still in the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the auto-filled sheet if asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the sheet the company sends, but I would want somebody to show me what changed. I am not going to guess at an isolation point to save a minute.

say: I would ask whether **software orders** bring the right fuse and address.
I would challenge **shorter repair targets** when site conditions are missing.
think: I expect my **hands-on line work** to continue while office buying jobs shrink.
A cut to **standby shifts** could reduce pay even if the job remains.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** and request the old and new time targets.
Bring **three site examples** with other crews to a staff meeting.
feel: I feel **skeptical**, but the savings cushion prevents immediate distress.
S1.quote: A single green tick on a computer would not show the wet ladder.
fieldNote: Daria expects **office cuts** before physical field cuts, but watches for a smaller standby rota from unrealistic scheduling.
She would present **site-level evidence** with other crews, avoiding a general argument about technology.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts during the planning rollout
Bring three logged site examples with other crews to the staff meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the depot can buy planning software if it really brings the right parts. A wrong address or fuse size still leaves a crew waiting in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying and booking jobs could shrink first, while I expect to keep repairing lines. The worry for me is a manager using a tidy screen to claim our work takes half the time, then trimming the standby rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking my paid shifts and ask the supervisor for the old and new repair-time targets. During the first year I would log three jobs where the software missed site conditions and bring the examples to a staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel skeptical, but not desperate. Our savings would cover a short disruption, though I do not want to spend them because a timetable ignored what we found on a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put beside each example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record the permit number, the part we actually needed and the time spent making the site safe. A single green tick on a computer would not show the wet ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a staff meeting instead of a private complaint?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If three crews bring their examples, the supervisor has to compare the targets with real repairs. I would speak plainly, without turning it into a fight about technology in general.

say: I would distinguish **2028 work orders** from field robots around 2031.
I would demand a **damaged-pole trial** before reducing van crews.
think: At **48**, capable robots could take physical line shifts.
My **two-month reserve** would not carry a long wage gap, despite other employers nearby.
do: Keep paid **repairs** in 2029 and seek another line vacancy if hours fall.
Replace the children's **paid climbing visit** with a public park outing.
feel: I feel **tense about 2031** while waiting for real crew decisions.
S2.quote: Two months saved would disappear fast if the company cut crews, although there are a few other line employers within driving distance.
fieldNote: Daria recognizes a **three-year gap** before physical robots, keeping paid repairs rather than treating 2028 as immediate field job loss.
Her **cash reserve** buys only limited time, so she names a precise family cut and a conditional nearby job application.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through 2029
Apply for a posted nearby line vacancy if field hours fall
Replace the monthly paid climbing wall visit with a public park outing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that full thinking AI in 2028 could write every work order, but robots able to fix lines arrive around 2031. I would want to see a robot repair a damaged pole before anyone takes a person off the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the office changes and 48 when robots reach the field. Two months saved would disappear fast if the company cut crews, although there are a few other line employers within driving distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask our supervisor for the robot trial schedule and keep my regular repair rota. In 2029 I would take the paid shifts available, apply for a posted line vacancy at another utility if our hours fell and stop paying for the children's extra weekend activity until we knew more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel tense about 2031, not about a form in 2028. I would tell the children only that we are changing the weekend plan, because I do not know whether my job will actually go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which weekend cost would you remove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children both go to a paid climbing wall once a month. We could take them to the public park instead and leave the savings account untouched for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train for a different job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a local employer offered paid practical training with a job at the end, I would listen. I would not quit a known wage for a course delivered on a screen.

say: I would ask for **storm-damaged pole trials** before field staffing changes.
I would separate **2031 office AI** from line robots around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still need a wage for the mortgage.
A **desk maintenance title** could disappear if full AI checks reports.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** in 2032 and ask about real field maintenance posts.
Watch a paid **robot trial** and apply for a comparable field vacancy.
feel: I feel **less pressed** with time to see a real job opening.
S3.quote: A photograph of a tidy joint would not tell me whether the line is safe.
fieldNote: Daria considers a **nearby utility** only for a posted field role with comparable pay, consistent with her reluctance to risk familiar work.
She rejects **report-checking safety** after full AI and wants actual isolation and testing shown in poor weather.

steps.text: Apply for a comparable posted field maintenance job if available
Take paid hands-on training if required for the posted field role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives the company time to test a robot on a storm-damaged pole, not only on a straight training span. Thinking AI reaches the office in 2031 and field robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 in 2031 and 51 when robots arrive. My older child might be finishing school, but the mortgage will not vanish on a birthday and I cannot assume I could retire at 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask a neighbouring utility what field maintenance posts they actually recruit for and keep my present shifts. In 2032 I would watch a robot trial on paid time, apply for a posted field maintenance role if pay matched and accept paid hands-on training if that role required it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed than in the fast picture. I could move to another field job, but I need to see a real vacancy before learning new controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the neighbouring utility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether their maintenance crews still work at poles or mostly sit with reports. Full AI could do report checking, so I would not mistake a desk for safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the crew to show the isolation, the repair and the final test in poor weather. A photograph of a tidy joint would not tell me whether the line is safe.

say: I would request **yearly paid field hours** before judging robot staffing.
I would distinguish **2036 office AI** from line robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, I cannot assume grown children clear the mortgage or fund retirement.
A **nearby field vacancy** matters only if my own hours fall.
do: Keep paid **line repairs** in 2037 and review yearly hours with my partner.
Apply for a **posted field role** elsewhere only if my rota shrinks.
feel: I feel **steady for now** and watchful about the later robot date.
S4.quote: I would not count leaving our two-month emergency fund alone as adding to our savings.
fieldNote: Daria expects **continued paid physical work** across the near years and uses field-hour reports as her trigger for moving.
Her **two-month reserve** stays available for emergencies; she does not claim existing money is new saving.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs through 2037 and review yearly hours
Apply for a posted field role at another utility if her rota shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that ten years gives us enough repair records to judge the machines properly. Full AI changes office work in 2036; robots that can do line repairs arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking date and 56 when robots arrive. The children may be grown, but I cannot assume the mortgage is paid or that retirement at 56 is an option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would stay on the repair rota and ask once a year how many field hours the company still pays. In 2037 I would keep working the line, review the figures with my partner and apply for a posted field role at another utility only if my own hours began falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about the near years. A decade lets me stay with work I know, and two months of savings gives a little time if a later transfer becomes necessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you increase the savings balance now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already hold two months of expenses, and I would keep it for emergencies. I would not count leaving our two-month emergency fund alone as adding to our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children as adults?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that a trade is worth learning with eyes open. I would not promise them my exact job will still exist after the robot trials.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because line-capable robots could arrive around 2031, and two months saved is not a long runway for a mortgage. Honest poor-weather trials, a posted nearby field vacancy and paid hands-on training tied to the job would help me choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether field jobs at nearby utilities would still be open once robots arrive everywhere. A vacancy today is useful; an imagined vacancy in five years is no plan.

headlineQuote: A vacancy today is useful; an imagined vacancy in five years is no plan.
portrait: Daria is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She has **never used AI** and trusts printed permits, pole numbers and direct field tests.
Her **two-month reserve**, typical pay and some nearby employers give limited room for a job search.
Across the scenarios she seeks **posted field work** and practical trial evidence before leaving a familiar rota.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** leaves about three years before robots could cut her physical line hours.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **poor-weather trials**, a posted nearby field vacancy and linked paid training would help her decide.
